newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish "vampire" gets 25 years for murder.
newsitem.headline: Polish "vampire" gets 25 years for murder.

text.p: One of Poland's most gruesome and baffling serial murder trials ended on Monday with the conviction of Leszek Pekalski for the killing of one woman and his acquittal on 16 other murder charges for lack of evidence.

A court in Slupsk, in northwest Poland, sentenced the chubby, crop-haired former bricklayer to 25 years in prison for a single 1991 sex murder, ruling that the jail term should start only after he has been treated in a psychiatric hospital.
"He was found guilty of one killing," court secretary Marzena Lecka told Reuters.

During a three-year investigation, Pekalski at first admitted to almost 70 murders, then cut the number to 14 -- which he repeated in interviews with journalists -- and finally denied any killings at all and alleged that police had pressured him into making false confessions.

When he entered the court on Monday, the man dubbed by reporters the "Bytow Vampire" after his home town near Slupsk and the savagery of his alleged crimes, faced 17 charges of murder, two of rape and one for the abduction of a baby who later died of cold.
In all but one of the cases, his lawyers successfully pointed to a lack of confident witnesses and of unambiguous evidence other than Pekalski's admissions which were later withdrawn.

Prosecutors said Pekalski had attacked his alleged victims, mostly women, with exceptional cruelty -- beating and kicking them, strangling them with his hands and items of clothing, using knives or wooden clubs, and sexually assaulting them.
He was found guilty of killing a woman identified, according to Polish legal practice, only as Sylwia R. whom he also sexually assaulted and robbed near Slupsk in 1991.
Lecka said Pekalski, who has calmly posed for cameras throughout the trial which began in April, reacted with apparent indifference to the sentence.

In his final statement to the court, in which he repeated his not-guilty plea, Pekalski asked that if convicted he should be sent to a hospital far from his home town for fear of attack by relatives of murder victims.
